ExplanationParts.CorpusEarnedOpening: The expression denotes one arrowhead pierces three checkpoints in these Chan records. Its wording is ‘one arrowhead pierces three checkpoints.’ In Qinshan Wensui's exchange, Juliang asks what it is like when one arrow pierces three checkpoints; Qinshan answers, ‘release Qinshan Wensui within the checkpoints and let me see.’ After Juliang calls it a good arrow shot in the wrong place, Qinshan seizes him and says to set piercing three checkpoints aside and shoot an arrow for Qinshan; Juliang hesitates and is struck seven times.
EvidenceBody: Yunmen gives the whole phrase as his own answer after asking how to undertake ‘covering heaven and earth, weighing the coming mechanism to the fraction’ without involving worldly conditions and receiving no answer from the assembly. Later teaching-seat records take up the same archery line with staffs, calling it a flash-like edge, and verse uses it as a closing line. The Zen bend is the military checkpoint-and-arrow formula's repeated use as an answer, challenge, and teaching-seat line in public encounter. The records do not define a universal set of three checkpoints here, so this entry does not substitute Huanglong's or Doushuai's named threes.
